summary: Updates the specification of the WHOIS protocol and obsoletes RFC 954, removing material that has nothing to do with the on-the-wire protocol or is no longer applicable. It does not try to change the protocol itself.

plainLanguage.summary: WHOIS lets a client ask a server for information using a short text request. The server replies with human-readable text and closes the connection to show that the answer is complete.

questions: how does a whois response end
subtitle: Defines the text-based WHOIS query and response exchange over TCP.

tldr.problem: WHOIS needed a concise description of its on-the-wire exchange, separate from older material that no longer applied.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a text query terminated by carriage return and line feed to a server on TCP port 43. The server returns text and closes the connection when its response is complete.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3912 documents the protocol without changing it and obsoletes RFCs 954 and 812. It notes that WHOIS lacks strong security and a defined character-set mechanism.

today: RFC 3912 is listed as a Draft Standard and obsoletes RFC 954 and RFC 812, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: What WHOIS Provides
sections.content:
WHOIS is a TCP-based query-and-response protocol. It delivers its answers as human-readable text and has been used for information services, including registered domain-name information.

This RFC records the protocol as it exists. It removes older material that is not part of the wire protocol and does not define newer uses of WHOIS.
sections.plainLanguage: A WHOIS client asks a server for information, and the server sends back readable text. This RFC describes the exchange rather than changing the protocol.

sections.title: The Query and Response
sections.content:
A WHOIS server listens on TCP port 43. The client sends a text request ending in ASCII carriage return and line feed. The server returns text, which may contain several lines.

Line endings do not mark the end of the response. The server closes the TCP connection when it has finished sending output, and that close tells the client the response is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a line of text to the server on port 43. The server's connection close, not a line break, marks the end of its answer.

sections.title: Character Sets and Security Limits
sections.content:
WHOIS has no mechanism for naming the character set used in a request or response. Although US-ASCII was originally predominant, the RFC notes that some servers may use other character sets, which can harm interoperability.

The protocol has no access control, integrity, or confidentiality mechanisms. The RFC therefore says WHOIS services should be limited to information that is non-sensitive and intended for public access.
sections.plainLanguage: WHOIS does not identify which character set its text uses, so clients and servers may interpret text differently. It also does not protect information, so the RFC limits it to public, non-sensitive data.

references.text: Harrenstien, K., Stahl, M., and E. Feinler, "NICNAME/WHOIS", RFC 954, October 1985.
